Ekalaka received 8-10 inches of snow along with blizzard conditions. Many livestock and new born calves were buried in the snow. Records show $1,049,659 in losses for livestock in Carter County. This figure does not include what would be an average death loss during calving season, this was above and beyond the usual. This number is from about 140 livestock producers in the county. About 60 more producers probably had losses, but did not report or may not have hit the threshold for reporting. The average for producers reporting was about $7500 of loss. It was very stressful for ranchers with back-to-back storms with snow so deep there was no place left to put livestock. However, there were no serious power outages and no lives lost or serious injuries to residents. |In addition, road damage was severe with the county losing two bridges due to flood damage as the snow rapidly melted due to a quick warm-up after the storm. Smaller creeks flooded and Highway 566 was closed from Birney to Ashland due to water and debris running over the road. Road damage was reported throughout Custer County.

Heavy rainfall also caused numerous roads and culverts to wash out in Custer County. A five day total of 4.08 inches at Volborg was reported on the 25th . On the morning of May 25th, a cooperative observer reported that Pumpkin Creek was out of its banks 5 miles north of Volborg with low land flooding. In addition, runoff from recent heavy rains also caused water levels to rise on the Tongue River below the Twelve Mile Dam.

The Bowler Flats tornado was on the ground for approximately one mile and lasted for five minutes. The tornado destroyed four transmission structures, damaged a transmission pole, shredded two wooden power poles and damaged some fencing.|Otherwise, it remained over open areas. Damage consisted of a house roof and front porch blown off, broken windows, as well as the house being shifted off of its foundation. Winds were estimated at 111-135 mph.

At approximately 345pm to about 352pm, a supercell thunderstorm produced a tornado with surrounding microburst damage occurred about 15 miles northeast of Wilsall over the foothills of the Crazy Mountains in Park County. Thousands of trees were damaged, including large trees that were uprooted or snapped off at the base. Trees as large as three to four feet in diameter were uprooted and/or snapped. EF-2 scale damage with estimated wind speeds up to 120 mph was determined with this tornado.

Based on the observed damage, the tornado was classified as an EF-2 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Wind speeds within an EF-2 tornado range from 111-135 mph, and the associated damage observed at the Billings MetraPark and nearby businesses was consistent with this classification. The damage path was 120 yards wide with a length of about a half mile and on the ground an estimated 12 minutes.||The damage assessment and eyewitness accounts indicate that the tornado developed near the intersection of Lake Elmo Drive and Main Street in the Billings Heights at approximately 4:24 pm, with significant EF-2 damage to several nearby businesses. Damage included rooftops being blown off of three structures, windows blown out, power poles downed, business signs and billboards blown down along with several trees uprooted. The tornado appeared to weaken slightly as it progressed southeast across Alkali Creek. Limbs were broken off numerous trees in the vicinity of the creek. The tornadic circulation then appeared to have strengthened once again as it moved south over the Rimrock Auto Arena at Metrapark. EF-2 damage was again observed to the arena with much of the roof blown off along with other damage to the exterior of the building. Debris from the arena impacted other nearby businesses creating additional damage, mainly in the form of broken windows. Debris from the arena was reported landing as far away as a mile from the tornado touchdown. The tornado then dissipated over the arena around 4:36 pm.||The associated thunderstorm then moved northeast away from Billings. Numerous sightings of funnel clouds were reported as this storm moved east-northeast of Billings, however no additional tornado touchdowns were reported.

Widespread flooding resulted in road closures occurring across Custer County with numerous roads reported as washed out. Significant flooding was reported along the Powder River as well as its tributaries. Dry, Spring, Strevel and Mizpah Creeks all reported flooding. Major flooding occurred from north of Powderville to Mizpah. Water overtopped Pumpkin Bridge on Pumpkin Creek. A storm spotter 16 miles south of Miles City on Highway 59 indicated this was the worst flooding that they had seen in that area in 25 years. There was significant lowland flooding in the Yellowstone Valley area of Northeast Miles City where Emergency Travel Only was declared for a time. A water rescue was required when a paper carrier in the valley washed off the road. ||Tongue River flooding on May 10-11th resulted in Custer County declaring a flood disaster and a water rescue due to Graveyard Creek washing out Kinsey Road. A levee system was damaged in Miles City. In addition, Custer County ran out of road closed signs due to extent of washed out roads.
Several roads across Treasure County flooded, especially northeast of Hysham area.

Significant small stream flooding across much of Fallon County. Numerous roads closed and eventually washed out with additional damage reported to several bridges. Water breached a small dam and a couple private holding ponds in the region. Significant erosion threatened the Waste Water Treatment Plant in Baker. Significant flooding reported on O'Fallon Creek where one spotter reported the highest levels on the stream in at least 58 years with over a foot of water covering much of their farmland.  At the Boxelder and Horse Creek confluence, flood waters rushed over dikes and into hayfields. Floodwaters surrounded one house in that region. Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Record to near record flooding reported on rivers and streams across Carter County. A total of 10 homes were reported as damaged by floodwaters. Damage estimates were based on FEMA reports and Individual Assistance approvals. On Boxelder Creek, at it's highest levels, water was flowing across Highway 277 between Hammond and Ridgeway and across Highway 323 (3 miles north of Belltower) about a half mile wide in spots. On the Little Missouri River, record flooding was reported. Significant flooding noted in the Albion area where one individual had to be rescued as floodwaters surrounded their house. Two dams also breached due to the high waters. Widespread farmland flooding occurred along Thompson Creek in southern Carter County between Ridge and Alzada. Significant erosion and flooding occurred along numerous small stream tributaries all across the county due to the rapid rainfall rates, resulting in considerable damage to county roads. At one point, Hammond Road between Hammond and where it intersects Highway 323 just northeast of Ridgeway was flooded in 7 different places.

Significant flooding occurred on creeks and streams across Carbon County with numerous county roads flooded, closing roads and resulting in significant damage. Emergency Travel only was advised at one point due to the severity of the flooding. Specifically, Rock Creek flooded, resulting in adjacent lowland flooding and closure of Grape Vine Road near Fromberg. Creeks were running out of their banks from the Beartooth Foothills between McLeod and Red Lodge, as well as tributaries of the Clarks Fork of the Yellowstone River from Belfry to Bridger. Five Mile Creek flooded and washed out the bridge on East Pryor Road between Edgar and Pryor. Blue Water Creek east of Bridger flooded and washed out a county road as well. The heavy rainfall also resulted in water running over the spillway at Cooney Dam. This resulted in several homes flooded along Red Lodge Creek. ||On May 25th, significant flooding was reported in the town of Joliet as debris backed up Rock Creek resulting in evacuations. At the peak of this flooding, Highway 212 was closed from Rockvale to Red Lodge as 18 inches of water was reported on Highway 212 through the town of Joliet. Fifty homes flooded in the area and seven people, mainly elderly, had to leave with the assistance of the fire and sheriffs offices. The Joliet Motel reported a foot of water in each of their rooms. ||In addition, an 84-year-old woman drowned after she fell into a flooded ditch near her house. She was going to get her newspaper when she slipped and fell. The woman was swept a short distance downstream from her house near Boyd, where authorities found her body.||Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Significant flooding occurred all across Stillwater County, including streams and creeks emerging from the Beartooth Foothills. This resulted in numerous road closures and significant damage in spots to rural roads. Specifically; Whitebird, Benbow, and the Stillwater River roads were closed. During the height of the flooding, a couple of families were stranded by the flood waters. A bridge was washed out on Whitebird Creek. Subsequent flooding on the Stillwater River was observed the May 24-25th. Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Significant flooding occurred on creeks and streams across Sweet Grass County resulting in widespread lowland flooding and numerous county roads flooded, closing roads and resulting in significant damage. Numerous bridges also washed out. Specifically, Upper Deer, Lower Deer, Bridger, Sweet Grass, Big Timber and Otter Creeks Flooded. Specific roads flooded include; Anderson, Lower Sweet Grass, Mendinhaul, and Windsor Loop. At the height of the flooding, water was overtopping Interstate 90 from Mile Post 376 to 377. Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Persistent rainfall combined with snowmelt in the mountains resulted in significant flooding along the Musselshell River. The Musselshell River at Harlowton rose above flood stage from May 22nd through May 30th. The river crested at 7.47 feet on the 22nd and again on the 29th at 10.25 feet which was a record stage. In addition, the Musselshell River at Shawmut crested at a record 9.27 feet on May 26th. Extensive lowland flooding resulted along the Musselshell River as well as its tributaries. Numerous roads were closed by floodwaters with many of those eventually washing out.  Flooding persisted into the month of June. Damage estimates were not available.

Very heavy rainfall combined with high elevation snowmelt the second half of May 2011 maintained some flooding into June along the Musselshell River. See May 2011 Storm Data publication for details regarding the significant flood impacts and damage estimates on this particular flood event.

Persistent rainfall combined with snowmelt in the mountains resulted in significant flooding along the Musselshell River and its tributaries, including the Ryegate area.  The Musselshell River at the gauge at Lavina crested at a record 14.04 feet on May 25th. Extensive lowland flooding resulted along the Musselshell River as well as its tributaries. As the water on the Musselshell rose quickly on the 24th, floodwaters quickly inundated Highway 12 east of Ryegate (Slayton Underpass) and at the height of the event, water was over Highway 12 in 3 different locations. Approximately 10 homes required evacuations due to the rapidly rising flood waters. One resident canoed in/out of their home for 2 weeks straight. Extensive flooding was reported in both Ryegate and Lavina where numerous homes and businesses were under water. A grocery store in Ryegate reported 3 feet of water both in and outside their business. Numerous roads were closed by floodwaters with many washing out. A bridge was also washed out east of Lavina.  Flooding persisted into the month of June. Damage estimates were based only on individual assistance approvals through FEMA. No dollar amount was available for infrastructure losses.

Very heavy rainfall combined with high elevation snowmelt the second half of May 2011 maintained some flooding into June along the Musselshell River. See May 2011 Storm Data publication for details regarding the significant flood impacts and damage estimates on this particular flood event.

Persistent heavy rainfall combined with snowmelt in the mountains resulted in extensive and significant flooding along the Musselshell River and its tributaries, including the Roundup area where record flows were observed. The Musselshell River at the gauge at Roundup crested at a record of 14.78 feet on May 26th. As the water on the Musselshell rose quickly on the 26th, floodwaters quickly inundated the town of Roundup. Portions of Highways 12 and 87 were closed in and around Roundup with up to 8 feet of water covering the roads in spots. This completely cut off the town from surrounding areas for several days. Homes and businesses in Roundup were inundated by flood waters with water up to rooftop levels in some cases. 39 homes experienced major damage and were complete losses. Another 110 homes and businesses experienced at least minor flood damage. Four teenagers were rescued from the high waters after they disobeyed orders to stay out of the area and then became stranded. Further downstream on the Musselshell River, another 14 homes were damaged by the flood in the town of Musselshell. In all, hundreds of families were isolated due to the floodwaters and severely damaged roadways. Railroad tracks were reported as washed out in spots. Musselshell County was reported as one of the worst hit counties in the state of Montana.

Very heavy rainfall combined with high elevation snowmelt the second half of May 2011 maintained some flooding into June along the Musselshell River. See May 2011 Storm Data publication for details regarding the significant flood impacts and damage estimates on this particular flood event.

Heavy rainfall caused significant lowland flooding of rivers and streams across Treasure County, including some flooding and damage to area roads. The most concentrated flooding occurred along Muggins, Boxelder and Sarpy Creeks feeding into the Yellowstone River. Sarpy Creek flooding impacted travel on Highway 10. Across the entire county, an estimated half dozen roads were washed out. Additional heavy rainfall of 1-2 inches on May 29-30th resulted in prolonged flooding into the month of June. Specific damage estimates were not known.

Heavy rainfall caused rivers and streams to rise significantly resulting in some flooding. High water caused difficult passage on the road going into the town of Rosebud and water covered Highway 12 in the Hammond Valley. At the height of the flooding, Highway 12 was closed due to flooding from Ingomar to Forsyth. ||The Yellowstone River at Forsyth went above flood stage with minor lowland flooding reported from May 22nd through May 29th. The river crested at 12.35 feet on the 24th and 12.18 feet on the 28th.||Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Water was reported to be flowing over Highway 313 near Soap Creek. Heavy rainfall impacted streams draining into the St Xavier area. In addition, a body was found in a flooded vehicle at the Koyamas Pond recreation area near the Big Horn River.

Heavy rain showers in the Billings area produced between one and two inches of rain between 3pm and 5pm. Flash flooding was reported in the city of Billings along Alkali Creek and in the downtown area. Erosion and debris flows were reported along the Rims as well, with mud and rocks flowing over parts of Rimrock Road and 27th Street. In addition, Billings set an all-time record rainfall of 3.02 inches, most of which occurred during the afternoon downpour.

Local law enforcement reported water flowing over Frank Road and Sugarland Roads with debris flowing down Sugarland Road in Sheridan. Water was also reported to be spilling over a dike towards Soldier Creek Road.

Excessive rainfall during the evening of the 24th resulted in the overflowing of a stock pond, as well as flooding along Soldier Creek in western Sheridan. Law enforcement reported some homes in the Downer Addition Subdivision were flooded.

Heavy rains of 3 to 5 inches in the Big Horn Mountains and Foothills caused area streams and creeks to rise and result in localized flooding. Small streams and creeks around Dayton were reported to be flooded. In addition, flooding was reported along the Tongue River and Little Goose Creek and on creeks in the Ranchester area resulting in the closing of some county roads. During the height of the heavy rainfall, Pass Creek Road, far northern Sheridan County near the Montana border, flooded and was eventually washed out. Several culverts were also reported as washed out.

Widespread rainfall of 2 to 3 inches with locally higher amounts fell across the Yellowstone County area during a two day period. Billings had its all-time daily rainfall record broke on May 24th with 3.12 inches. This was just a part of a record setting precipitation month for Billings which totaled 9.54 inches. This rainfall on top of an already wet month resulted in some streams and creeks over Southern Yellowstone County to overflow their banks. Flooding occurred on Blue Creek in the Briarwood area. Several homes and structures were surrounded by water on Aviemore Court where some voluntary evacuations occurred. In addition, the Briarwood Golf Course was inundated with water.||Pryor Creek was out of its banks resulting in water spilling over a dike in a low lying area of Huntley. Fly Creek near Pompey was out of its banks and flooded a roadway leading to town. Flooding occurred along most of Pryor Creek between the towns of Pryor and Huntley. In addition, county officials reported that Pryor Creek Road Bridge between Interstates 90 and 94 was washed out.||Blue Creek Subdivision at Jene Helene Avenue flooded many homes and the Briarwood Golf Club May 20th-22nd. This resulted in the Billings Fire Department issuing voluntary evacuation orders. In addition, flash flooding occurred in Billings on May 24th forcing many road closures downtown and causing large boulders to fall off the Rimrocks. Flooding from Pryor Creek inundated a Huntley neighborhood and destroyed Pryor Creek Road on May 22nd. ||The Yellowstone River at Billings went above flood stage on May 25th through May 26th. The river crested at 13.92 feet on May 26th. ||In addition, a man operating a backhoe trying to save his house, drowned near Pryor Creek. The roadway had washed out from underneath the backhoe.||Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Significant flooding occurred on creeks and streams across Custer County with numerous county roads flooded, closing roads and resulting in significant damage. At the height of the flooding, emergency only travel was advised due to the magnitude of the event. The Powder River near Locate rose above flood stage from May 10th through May 23rd. The river crested four times at 11.29 feet, 11.70 feet, 11.27 feet and 9.28 feet on the 10th, 21st, 22nd and 23rd respectively. In addition, Pumpkin Creek was reported to be flowing over Highway 59 southeast of Miles City. Pumpkin Creek had a record crest of 13.98 feet on May 20th and 21st. The Yellowstone River at Miles City went above flood stage from May 22nd through May 29th. The river crested at 14.74 feet on the 24th and 14.53 feet on the 29th. The Tongue River at Miles City rose above flood stage from May 11th through May 23rd and crested at a record 13.99 feet on May 21st. Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Very heavy rainfall the second half of May 2011 maintained some flooding into the early part of June before water levels receded. See May 2011 Storm Data publication for details regarding the significant flood impacts and damage estimates.

County officials and spotters reported flooding in the southern end of Ranchester on the Tongue River and Five Mile Creek. Several locations in Ranchester had high water with flooding in low lands and back yards of some homes. In addition, rises on the Tongue River caused the streams and creeks feeding into the river to rise as well.

Heavy rainfall in the foothills of the Big Horn Mountains resulted in high flows and localized flooding on all rivers and streams across Sheridan County. County dispatch reported Soldier Creek was out of its banks and flooding homes in Downer Addition subdivision on the west side of Sheridan.

Very heavy rainfall the second half of May 2011 maintained some flooding into the early part of June before water levels receded as county officials reported continued flooding on Muggins Creek in Treasure County. See May 2011 Storm Data publication for details regarding the significant flood impacts and damage estimates.

High flows along the Musselshell River from receding floodwaters from May quickly returned to flood as more heavy rainfall moved through the region. Rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches fell across most of Golden Valley County during the 6th and 7th of June. This caused rapid water runoff and more flooding similar to what was experienced in May. County officials indicated flooding in the town of Ryegate and water on Highway 12 near Ryegate. There were reports of several homes being flooded. In addition, a rancher 10 miles southwest of Ryegate received 5 inches of rain which washed out roads and caused flash flooding.

High flows along the Musselshell River from receding floodwaters from May quickly returned to flood as more heavy rainfall moved through the region. Additional rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches fell across much of Musselshell County during the 6th and 7th of June. This caused rapid water runoff and similar flooding that had just occurred in May. County officials indicated flooding in the town of Roundup. Several roads were washed out and many others closed due to the flooding. Highways 87 and 12 leading into Roundup were inundated and closed. Evacuations of about 30 homes occurred in Roundup. About eight feet of standing water surrounded the Busy Bee Cafe, a local landmark in Roundup. Many houses and businesses in Roundup were under several feet of water. An estimated 50 structures were inundated with water, some up to their rooftops. In addition, four teenagers had to be rescued from the high waters after disobeying orders to stay out of the area and then became stranded.

High flows along the Musselshell River from receding floodwaters from May quickly returned to flood as more heavy rainfall moved through the region. Rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches fell across much of Wheatland County during the 6th and 7th of June. This caused rapid water runoff and more flooding similar to what occurred in May. County officials indicated flooding occurred all along the Musselshell River. There was extensive flooding in Harlowton. Highway 12 was inundated and closed leading into Harlowton. The Musselshell River at Harlowton fluctuated above and below flood stage from the 7th through the 14th. The river crested at 8.65 feet on the 9th and 8.54 feet on the 10th.

At 535 pm, a tornado touched down 5 miles west of Albion, MT in far southeast Montana. The tornado was estimated to have remained on the ground for 15 minutes, traveling approximately 5 miles to the east northeast. The tornado produced periodic damage along a 100 yard wide path. The worst of the damage was located one mile north of Albion. A National Weather Service Cooperative Weather Observer located just north of Albion reported 50-60 trees that were snapped off, some as large as 2 feet in diameter. Two calves were also killed in this vicinity. Before the tornado lifted, 1.5 miles northeast of Albion, the tornado destroyed several grain bins, snapped off 4 power poles, flipped a semi-trailer on its side and produced minor damage to a nearby home. The tornado was classified as an EF-1, with estimated winds of 86-109 mph at its strongest point, one mile north of Albion.

Carbon County officials reported that a rancher was struck and killed by lightning in the Pryor Mountains. The Sheriff's department said a 54-year-old man was rounding up cattle for branding at a ranch about 12 miles east of Bridger when he and his horse were struck about 1:30 pm on June 11th. The man and his horse died at the scene.

Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Park County during the late afternoon hours of Tuesday July 26. A woman leading a horseback ride in a wooded area at about 530pm in the Chico area was struck by lightning. A man performed CPR on the victim before she was flown to Livingston Memorial Hospital then to Billings Clinic. Another woman was treated at the scene for burns while a 6-year-old girl was treated for minor injuries at the hospital. Two horses were killed in the incident. Lightning strikes were fairly isolated in the region at the time.

Big Horn County Coroner reported that a 3-year-old boy died after being left in a parked car for several hours in Hardin. The boy died during the late afternoon hours when temperatures were in the lower 90s.
A wind gust of 65 mph was estimated 4 miles southeast of Moorhead.
Quarter to golf ball size hail was reported along with winds estimated at 40 to 50 mph.

At approximately 845pm, a tornado briefly touched down at a residence 5 miles east of Molt. A 15 foot grain bin was destroyed, picked up and thrown into an outbuilding 50 feet to the southwest. Additional minor damage occurred to the siding and room on a nearby house.

At approximately 930pm, a tornado briefly touched down at a residence 5 miles west of Shepherd. The path of damage was about 50 yards wide and extended to the northeast for about 200 yards. A roof was torn off of a garage and a shed. Debris that was blown into a nearby house caused additional damage to windows and siding. Three power poles in the area sustained damage. In addition, a horse trailer was flipped on its side.
A thunderstorm producing 0.63 inches of rain in 20 minutes resulted in water over some roads just northwest of Columbus.
A thunderstorm producing between 5.00 and 5.5 inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and flooded homes in Ryegate.

An area of slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain to portions of Rosebud County. The county sheriff reported flash flooding on the north side of the Yellowstone River near Forsyth. Dry Gulch Creek, near Porcupine Creek, filled up and flooded. Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches was reported.

From May 21st and even continuing into the month of June, extensive severe flooding occurred across Big Horn County from the Little Bighorn and Bighorn Rivers, as well as creeks and streams. An Incident Command Center was set up in Crow Agency where the Crow Tribal Chairman declared a disaster. At the height of the flooding, the Big Horn County Sheriffs office is quoted as saying, there is water everywhere.  Hundreds of people were evacuated as flooding affected every community on the Crow Reservation. Fifteen to twenty homes were heavily impacted by the flooding.  Interstate 90 south of Hardin to the Wyoming State line was closed for five days (May 21-26). Water rescues were required on the I-90 frontage road south of Crow Agency. Highway 212 was also closed for a period of time and at one point had water 3 feet deep overtopping the roadway. Railroad tracks and numerous rural roads were washed out in the area. In addition, flooding near Hardin brought down telephone equipment that handles 911 and long-distance calls for major cities and towns in eastern Montana. ||The Bighorn River above Tullock Creek crested at a record 10.86 feet on May 23rd. The Little Bighorn River at Hardin rose above flood stage from May 22nd through May 27th and crested at a record 12.32 feet on May 23rd.||Damage estimates based on FEMA reviews and Individual Assistance approvals.

Heavy rainfall upstream on the Yellowstone River resulted in the Yellowstone River at Miles City to rise above flood stage. The Yellowstone River at Miles City rose above flood stage June 11th through June 30th and crested at 13.19 feet on the 12th and 14.01 feet on the 28th. The persistent high flows resulted in significant bank erosion along the river. However, no major impacts occurred as a result.

Rainfall amounts ranging from 4-6 inches resulted in significant flooding across Powder River County. Most tributaries feeding the Powder and Little Powder River reported flooding. The Little Powder River subsequently flooded with water reported as flooding Highway 59 in several spots. This flooding resulted in numerous roads being washed out. Flood damage estimates were based on FEMA reports and Individual Assistance approvals.

County officials reported significant flooding across Park County, especially along the foothill locations and on the Shields River in the northern part of the county. The Shields River and its tributaries experienced significant flooding with adjacent low lying areas under water. Some of the creeks that were impacted by high water included Mission, Billman, and Fleshman Creeks. County officials also reported that several roads were closed, damaged and eventually washed out by high water. During the height of the event, the Department of Transportation closed the eastbound lanes of Interstate 90 at Springdale due to water over the road from Peterson Creek.|Damage estimates were based on FEMA reports and Individual Assistance approvals.

Highway 212 was closed on Lame Deer Divide due to the road sliding down a hill. Significant lowland flooding was also reported along Rosebud Creek. Sandbagging efforts were required on the Tongue River to avoid flooding of homes in the St Labre and Ashland areas.

Extreme flooding reported on Keiser Creek, north of Columbus. A dramatic rise in water levels occurred in the region, estimated 6-7 foot rise in a matter of minutes. Local bridge washed out along with damage to a shop. Flooding worsened as a result of debris collection at a bridge. Several houses flooded in the area.

Heavy rainfall combined with snowmelt runoff resulted in significant rises on the Yellowstone River near Forsyth. The river fluctuated above and below flood stage from the 9th through the end of the month. The river crested at 10.95 feet on the 11th, 10.79 feet on the 18th and 11.88 feet on the 28th.

Warm temperatures combined with scattered showers and thunderstorms resulted in continued high elevation snowmelt. As a result, the Yellowstone River at Livingston fluctuated above and below flood stage from the 23rd through the end of the month. The river crested at 9.85 feet on the 24th and 10.15 feet on the 30th. This 10.15 foot crest was the second highest crest on record at Livingston, only surpassed by the 1997 record flood. The persistent high flows resulted in significant erosion along the river. Some damage occurred to the island road as water overtopped the road. However, no major impacts were reported.

Rainfall combined with snow melt caused the Tongue River near Birney to fluctuate above and below flood stage throughout the entire month. The river crested at 6.34 feet on the 1st, 7.30 feet on the 12th, 6.94 feet on the 18th and 6.95 feet on the 27th. The 7.30 crest on June 12th was the highest crest on record at the gauge site near Birney. Sandbagging efforts avoided flooding downstream in the St Labre and Ashland areas. Otherwise, mainly lowland ranch and farm land was impacted.
A large 10x20 foot horse shed was destroyed by outflow winds from showers and a weak thunderstorm.

County officials reported flooding along Rock Creek near 2 Mile Road which resulted in 2 Mile Road north of Red Lodge being closed. In addition, Rock Creek in Red Lodge rose above flood stage on the 29th and continued above flood stage through the end of the month. The river crested at 7.78 feet on the 29th.

Flooding from June continued into July along Rock Creek near Two Mile Road. Emergency repairs were needed on the Two Mile Bridge(which was closed) north of Red Lodge. Rock Creek was also reported to have cut a new channel and was as high as it has ever been. As a result, residents in 4 to 5 homes were stranded in the Fox area about 6 miles north of Red Lodge. In addition, another 3 homes were under water in the Wagon Wheel Estates which is about 3 miles north of Red Lodge. Western Ranch Estates near Roberts was flooded. In addition, Grapevine and Cottonwood Roads near Silesia were closed. Rock Creek at Red Lodge rose above flood stage on the 5th and continued to run above flood stage through the 7th. The creek crested at 7.54 feet on the 5th and again at 7.69 feet on the 6th.

Icy roadways appeared to have played a role in a one-vehicle fatal crash two miles north of Ranchester on Interstate 90 in Sheridan County. According to Wyoming Highway Patrol, the victim died after being ejected from the vehicle she was in after the driver lost control of the car on the icy roadway.

Three snowmobilers ascended a steep, narrow drainage above Fisher Creek on Henderson Mountain outside of Cooke City. The drainage delivered the riders into steep, open terrain on the northeast face. The victim climbed to approximately 9,800 feet where he triggered the slide. He was able to turn downhill, but was caught as he descended the slope. His head was buried 2-3 feet deep and the heel of his boot was sticking out of the snow. He was found and uncovered in approximately 10-12 minutes, but did not survive. The crown of the avalanche ranged from 1-4 feet deep and 300-400 feet wide. The slide ran a total of 1,000 vertical feet. The slope angle at the trigger point was 35 degrees, but increased to 40 degrees near the upper portion of the crown. The alpha angle was 33 degrees. The debris ranged from 7-10 feet deep near the toe of the slide. More detailed information can be found at www.mtavalanche.com.

A supercell thunderstorm developed very quickly in Eastern Carter County around 2:15 pm. The thunderstorm produced the first ever EF-3 rated tornado in southern Montana. The tornado first touched down at 2:27 pm around 13 miles southwest of Camp Crook, South Dakota, or about 10 miles southwest of Capitol, Montana. The tornado formed in the Sheep Mountains and eventually crossed Tie Creek Road as it moved slowly north. People lost site of the tornado as it entered Custer National Forest around 3:30 pm. ||The tornado was on the ground for an hour and traveled 10 miles and was reported to be a half mile wide at times. The tornado completely destroyed a trailer home, twisting and throwing debris over a mile. A small and old A-frame school house was completely destroyed, with debris blown 100 yards away, leaving only the basement behind. Six vehicles were picked up and tossed up to 200 yards. Around 20 power poles were snapped off with one pulled up out of the ground. In addition, 20 hay bales, weighing 3/4 ton a piece, were blown so far away that they were not recovered. A swath of trees on the north end of the track into the Custer National Forest was flattened by the tornado. There were no injuries or deaths from the tornado but two horses were killed. ||This was the strongest tornado ever recorded in the Billings National Weather Service area of responsibility.

The pre-storm environment for eastern Montana was such that severe weather was likely. Surface dew point values in the Baker area were in the lower 60s with strong southeasterly flow converging in the vicinity of a stationary surface trough. This area of strong surface convergence, which also separated moist rich air to the east and drier air to the west, played a critical role in the development of this short-lived tornado. ||Although no fatalities occurred , seven injuries, some requiring hospitalization, resulted from the tornado. Two homes were totally destroyed and 40 to 50 more sustained excessive damage. The city blocks located between South 5th Street East and South 10th Street East intersected by Texas Avenue were hit the hardest and sustained the most damage. Many power poles were broken resulting in power lines down and power outages. Single tree trunks were described to look like match sticks as they were stripped of all branches and leaves. ||Over 70 personnel came with boots on the ground from the surrounding tri-state area. The communities of Plevna, Ekalaka, and Wibaux, Montana, Marmarth, Rhame, Bowman and Beach, North Dakota, as well as Ludlow, South Dakota responded shortly after the tornado.  ||At the mesoscale level (2 to 2000 km in space), the interaction of pre-existing convergence zones or boundaries can serve as areas of storm development or enhancement. In some cases, pre-existing thunderstorms interacting with a boundary of converging surface winds can rapidly develop short-lived tornadoes with very little precursor indication from weather radar. The time scale of these events typically is on the order of a few minutes (0-10 minutes). ||In the case of the thunderstorms near Baker on Saturday, June 11th, evidence of these types of boundaries was observed.
